newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Princess Diana defends her call for landmine ban.
newsitem.headline: Princess Diana defends her call for landmine ban.

text.p: Briatin's Princess Diana said on Wednesday she was only trying to help when she called for a worldwide ban on landmines during her visit to war-torn Angola, a plea which unleashed a political storm back home.
"All I am trying to do is to help...That is all I'm trying to do," Diana told journalists who questioned her in the central Angolan town of Kuito on the criticism by British politicians.

Diana, on a four-day visit to one of the world's most heavily mined countries in support of a British Red Cross campaign to ban anti-personnel mines, later visited deminers at work in a minefield and detonated a live mine.
In Britain, a prominent member of Prime Minister John Major's Conservative Party rounded on the divorced wife of heir-to-the throne Prince Charles for being "very uninformed".
"The parallel of nuclear weapons comes to mind. The other parallel that comes to my mind is Brigitte Bardot and cats. It doesn't actually add much to the sum of human knowledge.
"This is an important, sophisticated argument. It doesn't help simply to point at the amputees and say how terrible it is," Peter Viggers, who sits on parliament's defence committee, told BBC radio.

Her call for an international ban on the "hideous weapons" has caused a stir because Conservatives believe it could be read as endorsement of the policy of the main opposition Labour party, clear favourite to win Britain's forthcoming election.

The government backs a ban on most anti-personnel landmines but says it must be international to be effective. In contrast, Britain's Red Cross -- and Labour -- want the government to declare a unilateral ban and to destroy all its existing stocks.

British Red Cross chief Mike Whitlam said in reaction to the critics: "I am surprised because we are trying to get to the same end, the total ban on landmines. I am disappointed at what people are saying. This visit was set up so that the princess could see for herself the aftermath of war and landmines.

"We need to let the world know not just the physical damage but also the economic damage that landmines cause," he told reporters, with Diana at his side on their visit to Kuito, one of Angola's most devastated towns in central Bie province.
The princess strolled past crumbled and bullet-ridden buildings, damaged in Angola's 20-year civil war.
An estimated 30,000 people died in Kuito in fighting between government troops and former rebel UNITA forces.
Diana, 35, then flew to the central highlands capital of Huambo, a city which changed hands several times between the until 1994 when the two sides signed a peace accord.

Casually dressed in three-quarter length yellow designer pants, a white cotton shirt and mocassins, she was welcomed by a small crowd of officers from the United Nations overseeing Angola's peace process.
On her way from the airport Diana, nicknamed "the princess of peace" by some Angolans, was taken past the former home of UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi who fled Huambo in 1994.

At Huambo's main hospital she was obviously distressed when a nurse removed the bed covers from one of the child victims of landmines, Helena Ussav, whose stomach was blown away in a mine blast last year.

After donning an armoured vest and visor as protection, the princess was escorted along a road next to a minefield where she watched deminers of the British-based Halo Trust at work. At the end of her visit she detonated a live landmine 150 metres (yards) away from her.
Red Cross organisers said the princess had been reassured that the area over which she walked was completely safe.
After a short lunch Diana stopped to talk to victims of landmines, many of them mothers with babies, at Huambo's only orthopaedic centre where artificial limbs are made.
